title: 01 — CI/CD Fundamentals
html:
01 — CI/CD Fundamentals

Platform-agnostic. Everything here applies whether you use GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, GitLab, or Jenkins — the syntax changes, the principles don't.

1. The three terms, correctly distinguished

Term Means The test
Continuous Integration Every change is merged to the mainline frequently (at least daily) and automatically built and tested Can any developer merge to main and get a verdict within ~10 minutes?
Continuous Delivery Every change that passes CI is deployable to production at any time, with a push-button release Could you release right now, in one action, with confidence?
Continuous Deployment Every change that passes the pipeline is released to production automatically, no human gate Does merging to main put it in front of users without anyone clicking?

⚠️ Most teams that say "we do CI/CD" have automated builds and manual deployments. That's fine — but be precise in an interview, because the follow-up is always "which one, and what stops you doing the next one?" The honest answer ("we have CD to staging, production needs an approval because of change-management policy") is a better answer than an inflated one.

Why CI matters at all: the cost of integrating a change grows superlinearly with how long it sits unmerged. Long-lived branches produce merge conflicts, semantic conflicts (both changes compile, together they're wrong), and a large risky release instead of many small safe ones.

2. Anatomy of a pipeline

flowchart TB
    subgraph FAST["Fast feedback — must be < ~10 min"]
      A[Checkout] --> B[Restore + cache dependencies]
      B --> C[Build — warnings as errors]
      C --> D[Unit tests + coverage delta]
      D --> E[Static analysis: lint, format, SAST]
      E --> F[Secret scan + dependency/SCA scan]
    end
    subgraph SLOW["Slower — post-merge or parallel"]
      F --> G[Integration tests — Testcontainers]
      G --> H[Build artifact ONCE — image or zip]
      H --> I[Sign + publish + SBOM]
    end
    subgraph DEPLOY["Delivery"]
      I --> J[Deploy Dev — automatic]
      J --> K[Smoke tests]
      K --> L[Deploy Test/UAT — automatic]
      L --> M[E2E + performance]
      M --> N{Approval gate}
      N --> O[Deploy Production — slot swap / canary]
      O --> P[Verify SLOs → auto-rollback on breach]
    end

2.1 Stage-by-stage: what each one is actually for

Stage Purpose Fails the build when
Checkout Get the source —
Cache restore Avoid re-downloading NuGet/npm every run — (a cache miss is slow, not fatal)
Build Compile with TreatWarningsAsErrors Any compiler warning or error
Unit tests Verify logic Any failure; coverage on changed lines decreases
Format/lint Consistency without review debate dotnet format --verify-no-changes finds drift
SAST Find injection, crypto, auth flaws in your code New Critical/High finding
Secret scan Catch committed credentials Any hit
SCA Known CVEs in dependencies New Critical/High with a fix available
Integration tests Real database, real HTTP boundary Any failure
Package Produce the immutable artifact —
Deploy Move the artifact to an environment Health check fails after deploy
Smoke test Prove the deployed thing responds correctly Any failure → auto-rollback

2.2 The speed rule

PR feedback under 10 minutes, or people stop reading it. When a pipeline takes 40 minutes, developers context-switch, batch changes, and merge on red "because it's probably the flaky test". The pipeline stops being a safety net and becomes a tax.

How to get there:

  • Parallelise independent jobs (build backend ‖ build frontend ‖ lint).
  • Cache aggressively — NuGet, npm, Docker layers.
  • Split test suites: unit on every PR; integration on merge; E2E and load nightly.
  • Fail fast — cheapest checks first, so a formatting error doesn't wait for a 6-minute test run.
  • Right-size runners. A bigger runner is often cheaper than developer waiting time.
  • Only build what changed in a monorepo (path filters, affected-project detection).

3. Build once, promote everywhere

                        ┌──────────────────────────┐
   main branch  ──────▶ │  BUILD (one time)        │
                        │  → myapi:1.4.7-abc1234   │  ← immutable, traceable tag
                        └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                     │  the SAME bytes
             ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
             ▼                       ▼                       ▼
        Deploy Dev              Deploy Test              Deploy Prod
        + dev config            + test config            + prod config

Why this is non-negotiable:

  • If you rebuild per environment, production runs an artifact that was never tested. Different NuGet restore, different base image digest, different transitive dependency version.
  • It makes rollback trivial: redeploy the previous tag.
  • It makes "what's in production?" answerable: one tag maps to one commit.

Corollaries:

  • Configuration is injected at runtime, never compiled in. No appsettings.Production.json baked into the image with real values — use environment variables, App Configuration, or Key Vault references.
  • Tag with the git SHA: 1.4.7-abc1234. Never latest in a deployment manifest — you lose reproducibility and rollback.
  • Store the artifact in a registry/feed, not on a build agent.

4. Branching strategies

Strategy Shape Best for Cost
Trunk-based Everyone commits to main (or very short-lived branches, < 1 day), behind feature flags Teams practising CD. The industry default for high-performing teams Requires flags, strong tests, and discipline
GitHub Flow main + short-lived feature branches + PR Most teams. Simple, works with CD Branches must stay short
Release branches GitHub Flow + release/1.4 for hotfixes on supported versions Products with multiple supported versions in the field Cherry-picking overhead
GitFlow develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*, main Scheduled releases, versioned desktop/on-prem products ⚠️ Heavy; a poor fit for continuous delivery to a single web environment

💡 Recommendation: GitHub Flow with short-lived branches and PRs, plus feature flags for anything risky. That gives you the safety of review with the flow of trunk-based development.

The key insight: feature flags decouple deploy from release. Deploy the code dark, enable it for internal users, then a cohort, then everyone. Rollback becomes a toggle (seconds) instead of a redeploy (minutes). This is the single highest-leverage practice in delivery.

⚠️ Flag debt is real. Every flag is a branch in the code and a combinatorial test case. Set an expiry date on each one and delete it after full rollout. A codebase with 200 live flags is unmaintainable.

Branch protection rules that matter:

  • Require a PR, at least one approval, and dismissal of stale approvals on new commits.
  • Require status checks to pass (name them explicitly — a check that isn't required is decorative).
  • Require the branch to be up to date before merging (catches semantic conflicts).
  • Require signed commits in regulated environments.
  • Block force-push and deletion on main.
  • Require linear history (squash or rebase) if you want a readable, bisectable log.

5. Versioning

Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): breaking / feature / fix. Essential for libraries and public APIs, where consumers depend on the contract.

For deployed applications, SemVer is often ceremony. What you actually need is traceability: 1.4.7+abc1234 or 2026.07.27.42. The build number plus the git SHA answers "what's running and what's in it".

Automating it:

  • GitVersion — derives the version from branch names and tags. Powerful, occasionally opaque.
  • Conventional Commits + semantic-release — commit messages (feat:, fix:, feat!:) drive the version bump and the changelog automatically. 💡 The best option if the team will adopt the commit convention.
  • Manual <Version> in Directory.Build.props + CI build number suffix. Simple and predictable.
<!-- Directory.Build.props — one place for all projects -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Version>1.4.0</Version>
    <InformationalVersion>$(Version)+$(SourceRevisionId)</InformationalVersion>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <ContinuousIntegrationBuild Condition="'$(CI)' == 'true'">true</ContinuousIntegrationBuild>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

ContinuousIntegrationBuild makes builds deterministic (normalised paths in the PDB), which is required for reproducible builds and Source Link.

6. Testing in the pipeline

Test type Where Gate?
Static analysis (compiler, analyzers, format) PR ✔ Blocking
Unit PR ✔ Blocking
Integration (Testcontainers: real SQL, Redis, etc.) PR if fast, otherwise post-merge ✔ Blocking
Contract (Pact, OpenAPI diff) PR ✔ Blocking on breaking change
Smoke (post-deploy health + one real transaction) After each deploy ✔ Triggers rollback
E2E (Playwright, critical journeys only) After deploy to test ✔ Blocking to prod
Performance/load Nightly or pre-release ⚠️ Blocking if the SLO threshold is breached
Security (DAST, penetration) Scheduled Ticket, not block
Accessibility (axe) PR on frontend changes ✔ Blocking on new violations

Coverage as a gate: ⚠️ never a blanket percentage — that produces assertion-free tests written to satisfy the number. 💡 Gate on coverage of changed lines not decreasing. It focuses attention on new code without demanding archaeology on legacy code.

Flaky tests: a flaky test in the blocking path is worse than no test, because it trains everyone to ignore red builds. Quarantine immediately, fix or delete within a sprint, and track the flake rate as a metric.

7. Deployment strategies

Strategy Downtime Infra cost Rollback speed Use for
Recreate Yes 1× Redeploy Dev; or when two versions genuinely can't coexist
Rolling No 1× Gradual Default for stateless services (K8s, VMSS)
Blue/green No 2× during deploy Instant High-risk releases; App Service slots are blue/green
Canary No ~1× Stop and shift back High-traffic user-facing services, gated on metrics
Shadow/mirror No Extra compute N/A Validating a rewrite against real traffic
Feature flags No ~0 Seconds Anything risky. Combine with any of the above

7.1 The rule that makes all of them work

Every change must be backward compatible for at least one version.

EXPAND    →    MIGRATE    →    CONTRACT
add the new    dual-write,      remove the old,
(nullable/     backfill,        after nothing
optional)      switch reads     references it

⚠️ Skipping this is why teams say "we can't roll back, the migration already ran." If v2 removes a column and you roll back to v1, v1 crashes. If v2 only adds, rollback is safe.

7.2 Applied to specific change types

Change Safe sequence
Rename a database column Add new column → dual-write both → backfill → switch reads → stop writing old → drop old (three releases)
Change an API response field Add the new field alongside → clients migrate → remove the old (with a deprecation header and a sunset date)
Change a message schema Additive only; version the message; consumers must tolerate unknown fields
Remove an endpoint Deprecate → monitor per-consumer usage → contact remaining users → remove
Change a config key Read both keys for one release, then drop the old

8. Database changes in CI/CD

The hardest part of continuous delivery, because a database has state you can't just redeploy.

Approach comparison:

Migration-based (EF Core, DbUp, Flyway) State-based (SSDT/DACPAC, Redgate)
You write The change script The desired schema
Diff is Explicit, reviewable Generated at deploy time
Data migration Natural (you write it) Awkward (pre/post-deploy scripts)
Risk You must get the script right ⚠️ The generated diff may do something destructive you didn't anticipate
💡 Preference Migration-based for application databases State-based where a DBA team owns the schema

Rules regardless of approach:

  1. Review the generated SQL, every time. dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent — the C# migration is not the artifact; the SQL is.
  2. Never EnsureCreated() in production. It bypasses migrations entirely.
  3. Never auto-migrate on app startup with multiple instances — concurrent migrations race. Run migrations as a separate pipeline step or an init container, once, before the app rollout.
  4. Migrations are forward-only in production. Write a compensating migration rather than relying on Down(), which is rarely tested.
  5. Long backfills go in a batched background job, not in a migration that blocks the deployment for 20 minutes.
  6. Test the migration against a production-sized copy. A migration that takes 2 seconds on 50,000 rows can lock a table for 11 minutes on 40 million.
  7. Online index creation: WITH (ONLINE = ON) (SQL Server Enterprise) or CONCURRENTLY (Postgres).
# The correct ordering in a pipeline
- Migrate database (idempotent script, one execution, with a timeout)
- Deploy application (which is compatible with BOTH the old and new schema)
- (later release) Contract: remove the old schema elements

9. Environments

Environment Purpose Data Deploy trigger
Local Inner loop Seeded / Testcontainers Developer
Dev / Integration Continuous integration of everyone's work Synthetic Auto on merge to main
Test / QA / UAT Verification, business sign-off Masked production-like, same schema, comparable volume Auto
Staging / Pre-prod Production-shaped final check; often a slot Production or a recent copy Auto
Production Users Production Approved pipeline only

⚠️ A staging environment with 1,000 rows tells you nothing about a query that dies at 50 million. Staging is only useful if it is shaped like production: same topology, same service tiers (or a documented difference), comparable data volume.

Environment configuration should differ in values, not in structure. If dev uses a queue and production uses a database table, you're testing a different system.

10. Secrets and pipeline security

The hierarchy, best first:

Approach Secret exists? Use
Workload identity federation / OIDC ❌ None Pipeline → Azure authentication. Always prefer this
Managed identity ❌ None Azure resource → Azure resource
Vault-stored secret fetched at deploy ✔ In the vault, audited Third-party APIs with no federation support
CI variable marked secret ✔ In the CI system Last resort; rotate on a schedule
Secret in source ✔ Everywhere, forever ❌ Never

Supply-chain hardening for the pipeline itself:

  • Pin third-party actions/tasks to a commit SHA, not a tag — tags are mutable and a compromised action can exfiltrate every secret the job can see.
  • Least-privilege token permissions on every job.
  • Don't run untrusted PR code with access to secrets. Fork PRs must not receive production credentials (see file 02 §9 for the pull_request_target trap).
  • Separate credentials per environment, so a dev pipeline compromise can't touch production.
  • Require approval for production deployments, and log who approved.
  • Generate an SBOM and scan images before pushing.
  • Sign artifacts (Sigstore/Notation) where the supply chain matters.

⚠️ If a secret leaks: rotate first, then investigate, then clean history. The credential is compromised the moment it's pushed; rewriting git history doesn't un-clone it.

11. Rollback

Your rollback plan must be tested, not theoretical. "We'd roll forward" is a plan only if you can build, test, and deploy a fix in less time than the outage costs — which is rarely true at 2am.

Mechanism Speed Requires
Feature flag off Seconds The change was behind a flag
Slot swap back (App Service) ~Seconds Blue/green deployment
Redeploy the previous image tag 1–3 min Immutable tags, artifact retained
Traffic shift back (canary/Front Door) Seconds Weighted routing
Restore database Minutes–hours ⚠️ Data loss between the backup and now

💡 Automate rollback on SLO breach. After deploying, watch the error rate and latency for N minutes; if they exceed the threshold, roll back automatically and alert. A human noticing takes far longer than a query.

12. Pipeline as code

Everything in the repo, versioned with the code it builds. No pipelines edited in a web UI — those are unreviewable and unreproducible.

Practice Why
Pipeline definition in the repo Reviewed in PRs, versioned alongside the code
Reusable workflows / templates One canonical build+deploy definition shared across services, not 30 copies drifting apart
Parameterised by environment The same template deploys dev and prod with different inputs
Lint the pipeline actionlint, az pipelines runs validate
Test pipeline changes on a branch Never debug directly on main

⚠️ The most common pipeline smell: copy-pasted YAML across 15 repositories. When you need to add a security scan, you now have 15 PRs. Centralise into a reusable workflow (GitHub) or template repository (Azure DevOps) from the second service onward.

13. Metrics — measure the pipeline, not the activity

DORA metrics are the standard, and they're what a mature interviewer asks about:

Metric Definition Elite
Deployment frequency How often you deploy to production On demand, multiple per day
Lead time for changes Commit → running in production < 1 day
Change failure rate % of deployments causing a degradation 0–15%
Time to restore service How long to recover from a failure < 1 hour

Plus the operational ones: pipeline duration (p50 and p95), pipeline success rate (a chronically red pipeline is broken tooling, not diligent testing), flaky test rate, and time spent waiting for review.

⚠️ Don't measure lines of code, commits, or "automation coverage". Those measure activity, not outcomes, and they're trivially gamed.

14. Common anti-patterns

Anti-pattern Why it hurts Fix
Rebuilding per environment Prod runs untested bits Build once, promote
latest tag in deployment No reproducibility, no rollback Immutable SHA-based tags
Secrets in CI variables Leak surface, rotation burden OIDC / managed identity
Manual deployment steps in a runbook Unrepeatable, error-prone at 2am Automate; the runbook should say "run pipeline X"
Snowflake environments "Works in test" IaC, no manual changes
A 45-minute PR pipeline People stop reading it Parallelise, split suites, cache
Flaky tests tolerated Red stops meaning anything Quarantine → fix or delete
Auto-migrate on startup Concurrent migrations race Separate migration step
No rollback plan Outages last as long as a fix takes Slots/flags/tag redeploy, tested
One giant pipeline for a monorepo 40 minutes to change a README Path filters, affected-project builds
Approvals as security theatre People click through without reading Approve on evidence (test results, canary metrics), not habit
Deploying on Friday afternoon Nobody available when it breaks Not a rule about days — a rule about having capacity to respond

15. Checklist — a healthy pipeline

  • PR feedback in under ~10 minutes
  • Build once; the same artifact promoted through every environment
  • Immutable, traceable tags (git SHA); no latest
  • Configuration injected at runtime, not baked in
  • Static analysis, unit tests, secret scan, and dependency scan all blocking
  • Integration tests against real infrastructure (Testcontainers)
  • Coverage delta gate on changed lines; zero known-flaky tests blocking
  • Database migrations run as a separate, idempotent step, reviewed as SQL
  • Every change backward compatible for one version
  • Zero-downtime deployment mechanism (slots/rolling/canary) with a warm-up
  • Post-deploy smoke test with automatic rollback on failure
  • Production requires approval; the approval is recorded
  • Pipeline authenticates to the cloud with OIDC, no stored secrets
  • Third-party actions pinned to SHAs; least-privilege job permissions
  • Pipeline definition in the repo; shared logic in reusable templates
  • DORA metrics tracked and visible

🔍 Interview angles

  • What's the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment? Deployable at any time with a push-button release, vs automatically released with no human gate.
  • Why build once and promote? Otherwise production runs an artifact that was never tested; it also makes rollback and "what's running?" trivial.
  • How do you deploy a breaking database change with zero downtime? Expand/migrate/contract across three releases, with the app compatible with both schemas in the middle.
  • How do you handle secrets in a pipeline? OIDC federation to the cloud, managed identity between resources, a vault for the rest; never long-lived credentials in CI variables.
  • Your deployment broke production. Walk me through the next 10 minutes. Assess impact → mitigate first (flag off, slot swap back, redeploy previous tag) → then diagnose → blameless postmortem with a systemic fix.
  • How do you keep a pipeline fast as the repo grows? Parallelise, cache, split suites by stage, path-filter in a monorepo, and right-size the runners.
